title: AI Chatbots Failed to Urge Emergency Care in About 41% of Vietnamese Scenarios Versus 15% in English
key_facts: Research presented at the American College of Gastroenterology's 2026 meeting in Nashville (9 to 14 Oct) found AI chatbots failed to recommend emergency care about 41% of the time in Vietnamese versus 15% in English.
The study, titled 'Does AI Speak Gastroenterology Equitably?', tested four large language models across the seven most common languages spoken in the US using simulated digestive-health scenarios.
It is a conference abstract, not a peer-reviewed paper, and used no real patients.
The ACG summary did not name the four models or report results for each language; gaps also appeared in several other languages and English answers were not error-free.
The abstract's listed author contact, Harika Dadigiri, MD, said fluent replies do not mean reliable medical advice and called language equity part of patient safety.
Medical Daily notes that about 72% of Vietnamese Americans aged 5 and over speak Vietnamese at home (Pew Research Center).
Only digestive-health emergencies were tested, so it is unclear whether the gaps appear for heart, stroke or children's cases.
quote_evidence: The tools failed to recommend emergency care about 41% of the time in Vietnamese, compared with 15% in English.
The findings come from a conference abstract that tested simulated digestive-health scenarios. It did not involve real patients, and it has not been published as a full peer-reviewed study.

why_it_matters_hint: If chatbot emergency advice is weaker in some languages, patients who rely on it could delay care; this early test used made-up cases only.
